newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu return may be last chance for calm in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu return may be last chance for calm in Zaire.

text.p: As Zaire appears headed for war and civil chaos, the symbolism of President Mobutu Sese Seko's return from treatment abroad may be a last chance to restore stability, political analysts say.

Mobutu's spokesman told state television the president, who flew to south of France on Monday, would return to Zaire after a few days' recuperation following two months of cancer treatment in Switzerland.

"This return at a time when part of the country is occupied by Rwandan, Burundian and Ugandan forces with the help of accomplices as much inside as outside the country will without doubt change many things both political and military," the opposition Le Potential newspaper wrote on Tuesday.
Zaire's ragged army has been beaten back in the east of the country by Tutsi rebels whom Zaire says are backed neighbouring Rwanda.
In the capital student demonstrators on Tuesday threw stones and attacked cars as they called for the resignation of part-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo.
Military officials say Mobutu's fabled charisma would have been enough to motivate his demoralised army which has lost much of two eastern provinces to ethnic Tutsis in a couple of weeks.
But the president is ailing, and by accounts of diplomatic sources, in no shape to assume the role of a commander-in-chief.
Even when he lives in Zaire, Mobutu is not a hands-on president, preferring the seclusion of his jungle palace in Gbadolite 1,100 km (700 miles) from the capital.
However, Mobutu is a skilled diplomat and has the power to strike deals and compromises with enemies in a way other Zairean politicians can only envy, the analysts say.

A friend of Rwanda's ousted Hutu rulers, some of whom are blamed for the 1994 massacre of up to a million minority Tutsis, he has been a protector of more than a million Hutus who fled to Zaire when Tutsis seized power after the genocide.
Mobutu's personal intervention halted the wholesale expulsion of the Hutus by Kengo's government in August 1995, when the army managed to throw out 15,000 despite an international outcry.
The presence of the Hutus in a region where ethnic Tutsis have lived around the Mulenge mountains since the late 18th century, is at the heart of the conflict in eastern Zaire.
Zaire says the Banyamulenge Tutsis are surrogates of the Tutsi-dominated Rwanda army accused by Zaire of crossing into its territory to hit armed Hutus.
For 30 years Mobutu has ruled his sprawling Central African state as a personal fiefdom through what his critics say is a potent mix of brutality, cunning and bribery.
Corruption and mismanagement have impoverished the economy of what should be one of Africa's richest countries, endowed with vast mineral resources and agricultural potential.
But the self-styled "guide", who in public sports a leopard skin hat as a symbol of his authority, has always boasted that without him Zaire would finally collapse.
"Mobutu's return is absolutely necessary to the country, the situation will ease and Zaire will be able to defeat the invaders. The crisis will pass," said teacher Claude Mansangu.
"Whether you like him or not Mobutu is the president and the only man who can bring the country together," he added.
Some diplomats doubted Mobutu was likely to return soon and saw the announcemnet as just intended to reassure Zaireans at a difficult time.
Crises have always been good for Mobutu who has often reaped rewards both at home and from foreign powers worried about the destabilising effect on the region of an explosion in Zaire.
Taking power in a 1965 coup Mobutu rallied the country by putting down local rebellions with the help of foreign mercenaries. Possible opponents were eliminated as traitors.
In the 1970s two rebellions in the copper rich southern Shaba Province were again put down with the help of foreign troops after poorly paid Zairean troops had fled.
Two rounds of army-led rioting and looting killed dozens in Kinshasa in 1991 and 1993 until Mobutu sent in his special presidential division to restore calm.
Political pundits, however, say it is unlikely that the elite division will be sent to the eastern battlefront at the expense of Mobutu's security.
